power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: iOS SHORTCUTS FOR EXPERIENCE SAMPLING 1 iOS Shortcuts as a Free, No-Code Tool for Event-Triggered Experience Sampling

text.text: Event-triggered experience sampling captures experiences when particular behaviors or contexts occur, but implementing automated triggers can require costly platforms or custom software.
Some events, like opening or closing another app on an iPhone, are especially difficult to use as survey triggers with available tools.
We describe how iOS Shortcuts, a free, pre-installed automation tool, can provide a no-code approach to initiating web-based surveys in response to device-detectable events.
Automations can launch surveys and pass contextual information through URL parameters.
We explain the workflow, provide reusable templates for several common designs, and demonstrate feasibility in a pilot study.
Mobile communication research increasingly uses the experience sampling method (ESM) to study life as it unfolds.
While ESM surveys are commonly administered at fixed or randomly selected times, event-triggered designs prompt a survey when a target event is detected (Lu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: While ESM surveys are commonly administered at fixed or randomly selected times, event-triggered designs prompt a survey when a target event is detected <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Lu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Such designs allow researchers to capture experiences at meaningful moments in everyday life, like after a social media session, upon receiving a message, or when arriving at or leaving a particular location, enabling research on digital well-being, interpersonal communication, and context-dependent media use.

However, implementing event-triggered designs can be more challenging than time-based sampling, as they require detecting specific events and linking them to survey delivery, often requiring costly commercial ESM platforms or custom-developed applications (Otto et al., 2024), which can be prohibitive.
text.formatted: However, implementing event-triggered designs can be more challenging than time-based sampling, as they require detecting specific events and linking them to survey delivery, often requiring costly commercial ESM platforms or custom-developed applications <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Otto et al., 2024)</ref>, which can be prohibitive.

text.text: On iPhones, Shortcuts offers an alternative.
Shortcuts is a free, pre-installed automation tool that allows users to configure automations in which events, like opening or closing an app, trigger predefined actions.

HCI researchers have begun using Shortcuts for digital wellbeing interventions (Purohit & Monge Roffarello, 2025; Scott et al., 2024), while recent work demonstrates its potential for collecting ambulatory data linked to naturally occurring behavior (Norwood et al., 2026).
text.formatted: HCI researchers have begun using Shortcuts for digital wellbeing interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Purohit & Monge Roffarello, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Scott et al., 2024)</ref>, while recent work demonstrates its potential for collecting ambulatory data linked to naturally occurring behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Norwood et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Building on these applications, Shortcuts can also be used to initiate surveys in response to device-detectable events and pass contextual information to surveys through URL parameters.
Compared with dedicated ESM platforms and custom-developed applications, Shortcuts offers advantages in cost and accessibility but also in the types of events that can initiate surveys.

Although existing platforms like m-Path and Avicenna support various forms of event-triggered sampling (e.g., when a participant manually triggers a survey or via a geofence), at the time of writing, they do not support triggering surveys immediately when participants open or close other applications.

Shortcuts, by contrast, provides direct access to app-opening and app-closing events through native iOS automations, allowing researchers to initiate surveys at these moments and pass contextual information through URL parameters.
This makes otherwise difficult-toimplement event-triggered designs accessible without developing custom applications or purchasing additional event-triggering software.
Researchers can also create and distribute reusable Shortcuts, customise actions, and incorporate conditional logic without programming expertise.
Although participants must load automations on their devices, and available triggers are limited by iOS, the approach substantially lowers barriers to implementing these designs.
In this article, we describe the implementation of event-triggered ESM using iOS Shortcuts, provide reusable templates and detailed instructions, and demonstrate its feasibility in a pilot study.
See https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24084106 for additional supplementary materials.
text.formatted: See <ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24084106">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24084106</ref> for additional supplementary materials.

text.text: Overview of the key components and workflow for event-triggered ESM using iOS Shortcuts.
Note.
Panel A illustrates the general logic of event-triggered ESM using iOS Shortcuts.
An event detected by iOS initiates a Shortcut, which opens a web-based survey and passes contextual information through URL parameters.
Panel B illustrates the setup and data collection workflow, distinguishing the responsibilities of researchers and participants.
Researchers prepare and distribute the Shortcut, while participants install it and configure the corresponding Automation on their devices.
Once configured, the designated event triggers the Shortcut, which opens the survey in the participant's browser.
Contextual information, including participant identifiers, can then be recorded alongside survey responses.
iOS Shortcuts enables automations that run when a specified condition is met.
An ESM workflow built with Shortcuts consists of three core components and one optional extension.

Triggers define the conditions that initiate an automation. iOS currently exposes triggers across five categories: event, travel, communication, translation, and settings triggers (see Appendix A for an overview).
When a trigger occurs, the automation runs a Shortcut, which contains the actions to be performed (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: When a trigger occurs, the automation runs a Shortcut, which contains the actions to be performed (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: For ESM, the key action is Open URL, which opens the survey in the participant's browser.

Auxiliary actions can capture timestamps, read system variables, capture information from system apps, or write log entries (either to a local location or to an online database, see Norwood et al., 2026) 1.
text.formatted: Auxiliary actions can capture timestamps, read system variables, capture information from system apps, or write log entries (either to a local location or to an online database, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Norwood et al., 2026)</ref> 1.

text.text: Build a survey on a platform that accepts URL parameters and configure embedded fields for each variable (e.g., id, timestamp, trigger, app, usage duration).
In the researcher's Shortcuts app, create the shortcut that includes an Open URL step pointing to the survey URL, with parameter values supplied from prior actions.
Configure any participant-specific fields, such as the participant ID, as Import Questions.

Distribute the Shortcut to participants via an iCloud link, which adds a copy to a participant's iPhone (When loading the Shortcut, participants provide the values specified in the Import Questions, which are inserted into the relevant fields).
In the participant's Shortcuts app, create a new Automation, select the desired trigger (e.g., "When Instagram is closed"), and set it to run the Shortcut.
Disable the "Ask Before Running" toggle so the automation fires silently.
Illustrative screenshots of iOS Shortcuts for event-triggered ESM.
Note.
Illustrative screenshots depicting the page to specify a Shortcut (step 1), the page to select the trigger (step 2), and the page to link a Shortcut to a trigger.

To illustrate how researchers can implement different experience sampling designs using iOS Shortcuts, Appendix B provides four worked examples with reusable (downloadable) templates and step-by-step instructions.
The first uses an app-close trigger to launch a survey immediately after a participant closes a selected application, allowing researchers to assess postuse experiences like affect or guilt.

The second uses time-of-day triggers to administer surveys at predetermined intervals, enabling researchers to assess fluctuations in experiences like social connectedness or communication demands throughout the day.

The third uses location-based triggers to launch surveys when participants arrive at or leave specified locations, allowing researchers to investigate context-dependent experiences like work-related communication demands during transitions between home and work.
The fourth introduces randomised timebased triggering, using a random delay within a scheduled window to assess momentary experiences like distraction or social interaction at less predictable times.
In Appendix C, we demonstrate the feasibility of another, more elaborate event-triggered design in a pilot study (n = 21) of immediate reactions following prolonged TikTok sessions.
An automation fired whenever a participant closed TikTok after at least 15 minutes of use, launching a survey with the user ID and session duration embedded as URL parameters.

Because this protocol triggered a survey only when TikTok was closed after at least 15 minutes of use, the implementation required a more advanced procedure than the templates provided in Appendix B. Session duration is not itself an available trigger and cannot be computed within a single automation because "App Opened" and "App Closed" triggers fire as separate events and cannot share variables.
We therefore bridged two automations via the clipboard.
When TikTok opens, a Shortcut writes the timestamp to the clipboard.
When TikTok closes, a second Shortcut reads the clipboard, computes elapsed minutes, and opens the URL if the duration exceeds the 15-minute threshold.
In this feasibility demonstration, each participant received a personalized closing Shortcut with their participant ID embedded in the URL, distributed via an iCloud share link.
Setup was completed with the researchers in person and took approximately 10 minutes.
Once configured, the automations ran throughout the 10-day period, yielding 279 observations without troubleshooting.

Although this personalized-link procedure was workable for the small pilot, it requires researcher-side configuration for each participant; for larger or remote deployments, participant-specific values can instead be populated from a single shared Shortcut using Import Questions.
Remote onboarding also appears feasible. Norwood et al. (2026), for example, used video instructions to guide participants recruited through Prolific through the setup.
text.formatted: Remote onboarding also appears feasible. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Norwood et al. (2026)</ref>, for example, used video instructions to guide participants recruited through Prolific through the setup.

text.text: Appendix C provides an overview of the data, implementation details, and lessons learned from the pilot.
While Shortcuts enable free implementation of event-triggered designs on iOS, the approach has several constraints.
Most notably, it only works on iPhones.
Cross-platform deployments require a parallel Android implementation, which is feasible through Tasker (a paid app) or Routines (built into Android system settings).

Trigger coverage is broader on Android, with notification-level events accessible to Tasker but not iOS Shortcuts (except for incoming email/messages), although stability and onboarding effort vary by device, manufacturer, and OS version.
The set of usable events is bounded by what the operating system surfaces.
For example, in Shortcuts, notification arrival and most in-app actions are not accessible, and even available triggers can miss edge cases.
For example, in our deployment, the "App Closed" trigger did not fire when the screen locked while TikTok remained the foregrounded app (as was the case for Norwood et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For example, in our deployment, the "App Closed" trigger did not fire when the screen locked while TikTok remained the foregrounded app (as was the case for <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Norwood et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Sessions ending in screen-lock were missed unless participants closed TikTok before locking.
Onboarding is an important consideration for larger or remote samples.
Import Questions allow participant-specific values to be automatically populated from a single shared Shortcut, avoiding the need to create individualized copies.
However, participants must still add the Shortcut and configure the Automation correctly, which can be supported by in-person setup or remote onboarding instructions (Norwood et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, participants must still add the Shortcut and configure the Automation correctly, which can be supported by in-person setup or remote onboarding instructions <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Norwood et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Larger deployments should therefore include clear setup materials and an end-to-end test to verify that triggers and identifying parameters are configured correctly.

iOS Shortcuts provides a free, no-code approach to event-triggered ESM that enables researchers to initiate surveys in response to device-detectable events that are not readily supported by conventional ESM platforms on iOS.

By linking these events to web-based surveys and passing contextual information through URL parameters, the approach expands opportunities to study mobile communication experiences as they unfold without developing custom applications or purchasing dedicated triggering software.
The approach is compatible with iPhones running iOS 15+, although the available triggers and participant-side setup impose practical constraints.

To facilitate access and reuse, Appendix B provides shareable Shortcut templates and step-by-step instructions that researchers can adapt by modifying triggers, actions, survey URLs, and embedded parameters.
These resources offer a flexible starting point for implementing a range of event-triggered and other experience sampling designs.
iOS Shortcuts implements automations that run when a defined condition is met.
Each automation is built around a single trigger that specifies the condition.
The available triggers fall into five categories (see Table A1 for an overview): Event, Travel, Communication, Transaction, and Setting.
text.formatted: The available triggers fall into five categories (see Table <ref type="table">A1</ref> for an overview): Event, Travel, Communication, Transaction, and Setting.

text.text: As of September 2026, across these categories there are 21 distinct trigger types (see https://support.apple.com/guide/shortcuts/intro-to-personal-automation-apd690170742/ios).
text.formatted: As of September 2026, across these categories there are 21 distinct trigger types (see <ref type="url" target="https://support.apple.com/guide/shortcuts/intro-to-personal-automation-apd690170742/ios">https://support.apple.com/guide/shortcuts/intro-to-personal-automation-apd690170742/ios</ref>).

text.text: Most triggers expose one or more configurable options that designate when, where, or under what circumstances the automation runs.
Overview of trigger categories.

Event triggers run an automation at a specific time of day, in response to an alarm, the user's sleep schedule, during an Apple Watch workout, or when a recognized sound is detected (see Table A2 for a complete overview).
text.formatted: Event triggers run an automation at a specific time of day, in response to an alarm, the user's sleep schedule, during an Apple Watch workout, or when a recognized sound is detected (see Table <ref type="table">A2</ref> for a complete overview).

text.text: Sleep triggers require a sleep schedule set up in the Health app.
Apple Watch Workout triggers require an iPhone paired with an Apple Watch.
Sound Recognition triggers require Sound Recognition to be enabled in the Settings app.
Event triggers.
Time of Day Sunrise Runs at sunrise, as determined by the user's current location in the Weather app.
An offset of 15, 30, or 45 minutes, or 1, 2, 3, or 4 hours before or after sunrise may be applied.
Sunset Runs at sunset, as determined by the user's current location in the Weather app.
The same before/after offset options available for Sunrise may be applied.
Runs at a specific time of day.
Repeat Sets which day or days the automation runs: Daily (every day), Weekly (on selected days), or Monthly (on a selected day of the month).
Runs when the user snoozes the selected alarm.
Is Stopped Runs when the user stops the selected alarm.
Alarms Specifies which alarm applies: Any (any active alarm in the Clock app), Existing (a specific saved alarm), or Wake-up (the user's wake-up time set in the Bedtime category of the Clock app).
Runs when the user begins winding down for bed.
Bedtime Begins Runs when it is time for bed.
Waking Up Runs when the Wake Up alarm goes off.
Apple Watch Workout Workout Type Selects one or more workout types that launch the automation, or Any Workout.
When Workout Selects when the automation runs relative to the workout: Start, End, or Starts or Ends (at both the start and the end).

Sound Recognition Sound Recognition of a selected environmental sound triggers the automation (appliance, baby crying, fire alarm, cough, doorbell, kettle, smoke alarm, cat, car horn, water running, dog, shouting, siren, glass breaking, door knock).
Travel triggers run an automation based on the user's location (e.g., arriving at or leaving a place, the time they typically begin a commute, or connecting to and disconnecting from CarPlay).
"Before I Commute" triggers require the user to have a contact card to be set in device Settings so that their Home and Work addresses are available to the device.

text.text: Communication triggers.
Email Sender Runs when the user receives an email from any of the addresses added to this field.
Runs when the user receives an email whose subject contains the specified phrase.
Account Runs when the user receives an email in the chosen account.
Recipient Runs when the user receives an email addressed to any of the recipients added to this field.
Runs when the user receives a message from any of the senders added to this field.

Designs requiring more sophisticated triggering or context can extend these templates in several ways.

Conditional triggering (e.g., firing a survey only after a session reaches a minimum duration) and compound events (e.g., the duration of an app session, which requires bridging an App Open and an App Close event) require additional logic within the Shortcut and, in some cases, the use of two coordinated Shortcuts that share state across automations.

Appendix C describes the design used in our feasibility implementation, in which the duration of a TikTok session is computed by writing the start timestamp to the clipboard from a first Shortcut on App Open, and reading it back from a second Shortcut on App Close.
The same pattern can be adapted to any compound event where the trigger condition depends on a state that must persist between two automations.

Following the technical setup, the participants were briefed verbally and in writing.

The briefing covered when to expect a survey, how long it takes (about 30 seconds), what to do if the phone is locked mid-session (close TikTok before locking), and an instruction not to delete the Shortcuts or automations during the study.
Participants were told that they would be sent removal instructions at the end of the 10-day measurement period.
The implementation yielded a multilevel dataset of post-session responses, with sessions (Level 1) nested within participants (Level 2).
Across the 10-day measurement period, the 21 participants generated 279 post-session responses, a mean of 13.28 per participant (range 1 to 32, SD = 8.44, median = 12).

Two fields originated in the Shortcut itself and arrived in Qualtrics via the URL parameters, namely the participant identifier (Pid) used to link post-session responses to the baseline survey, and the computed session duration in minutes.
All remaining variables were captured through self-report items in the post-session survey.
The session timestamp was recorded implicitly as the Qualtrics response start time, which was used to derive a time-of-day variable (morning, afternoon, evening, late night).
The baseline and post-session data were joined on Pid to produce a single analytical dataset.
One cleaning issue is worth noting for anyone replicating this approach.
The perparticipant hardcoding of Pids in each copy of Shortcut B is error-prone on the researcher side.

In our pilot, one participant's Shortcut was erroneously shared with the placeholder ID left unchanged (their Pid arrived as the literal string "X"), and three further cases involved Pids that were inconsistently recorded across researcher logs.
We resolved these by matching unmatched post-session response times against unmatched baseline completion times, but this is fragile.
Future deployments should avoid researcher-side hardcoding of participant identifiers where possible.
A more scalable approach is to configure the Pid field as an Import Question in a single master Shortcut, allowing the identifier to be entered or pasted when the Shortcut is installed.
Regardless of how the identifier is populated, we recommend an end-to-end test at intake to confirm that the expected Pid is received by the survey platform.
The dataset captured variation in both session-level experience and trait-level individual differences.

After excluding these sessions, session duration had a median of 22 minutes (M = 24.49, SD = 9.24), and immediate post-use guilt had a mean of 3.56 on the 7-point scale (SD = 2.09).
A null multilevel model predicting immediate post-use guilt placed approximately 34.8% of the variance at the between-person level, with the remainder within persons across sessions.
This is a pattern typical of intensive longitudinal designs and consistent with the appropriateness of multilevel modelling for these data.

To demonstrate that the data captured a meaningful session-level signal, we fit a parsimonious model regressing immediate post-use guilt on three within-person session-level predictors (perceived goal conflict, disengagement intention gap, reduced awareness) along with session duration and time of day, with a random intercept by participant (Figure C2).

Overall, the ioS Shortcuts setup performed reliably across the 10-day measurement period.
Once configured during the intake session, the two automations ran without participant intervention for the duration of the study, and participants required no troubleshooting contact mid-deployment.
That being said, three classes of issues are worth flagging for anyone replicating this setup.

Trigger fidelity at the operating-system level iOS does not expose perfectly reliable session boundaries, and the "App Opened" and "App Closed" triggers can miss or mis-time events in ways that affect data capture.
The "App Closed" trigger does not fire when the screen locks while TikTok remains the foregrounded app.
If a participant locks their phone mid-scroll and later unlocks into a different app, the close event from TikTok never registers, and no survey is triggered.
Briefing participants explicitly to close TikTok before locking the phone is a partial mitigation, but a residual under-capture rate is expected.

Researchers replicating this approach should expect both under-capture from missed close events and over-estimation of duration for a small number of sessions, and should apply a plausibility ceiling on session duration during data cleaning, treating the resulting exclusions as a known artifact of the trigger model rather than as substantive outliers.
Two aspects of the present implementation introduce risk that researchers should design around.
First, the clipboard is shared with other apps.
If the participant copies arbitrary text during a TikTok session, the start timestamp written by Shortcut A is overwritten and the duration cannot be computed for that session.
In practice this case is rare, because Shortcut A rewrites the timestamp on every fresh TikTok open and the relevant period is the duration of a single session.
A more robust persistent store can be substituted (e.g., writing to a single-line text file in iCloud Drive via the Save File action), at the cost of two additional actions in each Shortcut.
We accepted the clipboard approach as the minimal viable implementation.
Second, the per-participant hardcoding of Pids in our implementation produced reconcilable but non-trivial cleaning work.
Future deployments can reduce the researcher-side burden of editing and resharing participant-specific Shortcuts by using an Import Question to populate the Pid from a single master Shortcut.
This does not eliminate the possibility of an incorrect Pid being entered, so an end-to-end verification step remains necessary.
The implementation depends on behaviors that are specific to a particular version of iOS and to Apple's current automation API.

The silent execution of automations (the "Ask Before Running" toggle behavior) was introduced in iOS 15, and the available triggers, the structure of Magic Variables, and the iCloud share mechanism for Shortcuts have all changed across iOS versions over the last several years.
Future iOS releases may alter or restrict any of these behaviors.

Researchers planning to replicate this approach should verify on the current iOS at the time of their study that automations still execute silently, that the relevant triggers remain exposed, and that Import Questions and other participant-specific parameters are populated as intended when an iCloud-shared Shortcut is added to a new device.

This appendix provides four template Shortcuts covering four key event-triggered ESM designs in mobile communication research, together with the survey platform setup required to receive the data and step-by-step build instructions for each template.
Readers can use any of the four as a starting point and modify the trigger, the embedded variables, or the survey URL to fit their own design.
Appendix C describes a more advanced pattern using two coordinated Shortcuts to compute the duration of an app session.
This approach can serve as a basis for designs in which information captured by one automation needs to be used by another.
An event-triggered ESM workflow built on iOS Shortcuts can be decomposed into four components, as introduced in the main text.
The trigger specifies when the survey should fire, such as when an app is opened, when a time of day is reached, or when a location is entered.
The action is what the Shortcut does in response, which for ESM purposes is to open a survey URL in the participant's default browser.

The embedded variables are contextual data that the Shortcut passes into the URL as query parameters, allowing the survey platform to record information that would otherwise be unavailable inside the survey itself (e.g., the time of the triggering event, the participant identifier, the type of event that fired the trigger).
Control flow elements, including If conditions and computations, can be added when the design requires conditional triggering or compound events.
Each of the four templates provided in this appendix follow the same overall pattern.
The Shortcut consists of a short sequence of actions that constructs a URL with embedded parameters and opens it in the browser.

As an illustration of the feasibility of using iOS Shortcuts to implement an event triggered ESM design we conducted a pilot study investigating immediate post-use guilt after extended TikTok sessions.

While the focus is primarily on feasibility, the research concerned the potential within-person relationship between disengagement intention gaps (i.e., the temporal distance between when a user wanted to stop and when they actually stopped), perceived goal conflict during the session, the session duration, and reduced awareness during a session (i.e., loss of time, automatic use, limited recall), and perceived guilt about Tiktok use.
The pilot study involved 21 iPhone users aged 18 to 30 recruited through convenience sampling at a university in The Netherlands.

After completing a baseline survey (accessed through a provided URL with an embedded parameter with an ID variable) in-person, each participant loaded an iOS Shortcuts setup that automatically opened a brief Qualtrics survey whenever they closed TikTok after a session of at least 15 minutes for a 10-day period (with the same embedded participant ID as a parameter).

The post-session survey contained ten items covering immediate guilt (3 items), reduced awareness (3 items), perceived goal conflict (1 item plus), the disengagement intention gap (1 slider), purpose of use, and contextual factors (location and social context).
The setup used two Shortcuts and two Automations on each participant's iPhone.
Together they turned the act of closing TikTok after a long session into a survey trigger.
iOS Automations expose "App Opened" and "App Closed" as separate triggers, each firing its own automation, and they cannot share variables directly.

The OFF setting is important.
With it on, the participant is asked to confirm each automation before it runs, defeating silent measurement.

text.text: Two parameters were passed to Qualtrics as embedded data fields: 1) session_duration, the elapsed minutes from open to close, computed within Shortcut B, and 2) Pid, the participant identifier, hardcoded into each participant's copy of Shortcut B. These two fields were configured as embedded data in the Qualtrics survey flow.
The session timestamp was implicitly recorded by Qualtrics as the response start time, so additional time-of-day variables did not need to be passed through the URL.
Each participant completed a short intake session, lasting roughly 10 to 15 minutes, during which the researcher and participant set up the Shortcuts together.
Before meeting with the participant, the researcher prepared a unique participant ID (e.g., P101, P102, etc.).

Embedded variables enable one to pass contextual data into the survey URL as parameters. iOS exposes the current date and time, location, focus mode, battery level, calculated numbers, and arbitrary user-defined values, and these can be inserted into the URL via the Magic Variable mechanism.
The optional fourth component is control flow, which adds conditional operations, loops, and basic computations.

Participant-specific values can either be entered directly into a Shortcut or requested during installation using Import Questions, allowing a single shared Shortcut to be personalized for each participant.
